name: Erikson's Stages of Psychosocial Development
statement: Life unfolds through eight stages, each posing a crisis whose resolution shapes a person's strengths.
statementAccent: each posing a crisis whose resolution shapes a person's strengths
meaning: Erikson's stages of psychosocial development are eight sequential stages of human development proposed by the German-American psychoanalyst Erik Erikson, notably in his 1950 book Childhood and Society, which describe how the personality develops across the entire lifespan through a series of social and emotional challenges. Each stage centers on a characteristic psychosocial crisis, a tension between two opposing dispositions that the person must work through; resolving it favorably yields a lasting strength or virtue, while failing to leaves difficulties that carry forward. The eight stages run from infancy to old age: trust versus mistrust in infancy, yielding hope; autonomy versus shame and doubt in early childhood, yielding will; initiative versus guilt in the preschool years, yielding purpose; industry versus inferiority in the school years, yielding competence; identity versus role confusion in adolescence, yielding fidelity; intimacy versus isolation in young adulthood, yielding love; generativity versus stagnation in middle adulthood, yielding care; and integrity versus despair in late adulthood, yielding wisdom. Unlike Freud, whose stages ended in adolescence, Erikson held that development continues throughout life and is driven by social relationships and cultural demands. He also coined the influential term identity crisis. The theory remains a foundational lifespan framework, though its stages are approximate and hard to test.
mechanism: Erikson's theory works through a sequence of eight psychosocial crises, each tied to a period of life and to the social relationships that dominate it. A crisis is not a catastrophe but a turning point, a tension between a positive, syntonic pole and a negative, dystonic one, arising as new social demands confront the developing person. In infancy, the crisis of trust versus mistrust turns on whether caregivers provide reliable care; in early childhood, autonomy versus shame and doubt turns on the chance to exercise independence; in the preschool years, initiative versus guilt turns on taking on tasks and asserting purpose; in the school years, industry versus inferiority turns on developing competence; in adolescence, identity versus role confusion turns on forming a coherent sense of self; in young adulthood, intimacy versus isolation turns on forming close bonds; in middle adulthood, generativity versus stagnation turns on contributing to the next generation; and in late adulthood, integrity versus despair turns on looking back on life with acceptance. Favorable resolution does not mean eliminating the negative pole but achieving a healthy balance weighted toward the positive, and each such resolution yields a basic virtue, hope, will, purpose, competence, fidelity, love, care, or wisdom. The stages build on one another, so earlier resolutions shape how later crises are met.

examples.text: In infancy, reliable care fosters trust and the virtue of hope, while neglect fosters mistrust.
In adolescence the central crisis is forming a coherent identity, yielding fidelity, versus confusion about one's role.
In late adulthood, looking back on life with acceptance yields integrity and wisdom, while regret yields despair.

variants.name: Lifespan development

whyItMatters: Erikson's stages of psychosocial development are among the most influential frameworks in the psychology of the whole human lifespan, because they extended the study of development beyond childhood to embrace the entire life course, from infancy to old age. By proposing that each period of life presents a characteristic psychosocial crisis whose resolution shapes personality and yields a particular strength, Erikson gave a rich vocabulary for thinking about how people grow, change, and face the challenges of each age, from an infant's trust to an elder's search for integrity. His concept of the identity crisis of adolescence, a term he coined, entered common language and profoundly influenced how the teenage years and the search for selfhood are understood. The theory emphasizes the social and cultural dimension of development, in contrast to Freud's focus on biological drives, and it has shaped fields including developmental psychology, education, counseling, and gerontology. Although its stages are approximate and difficult to test empirically, Erikson's framework remains a durable and widely taught map of how a life develops through a series of formative challenges.

working.text: at each life stage confront a psychosocial crisis, a tension between a positive and negative disposition.
achieve a healthy balance favoring the positive pole, drawing on how earlier crises were resolved.
from a favorable resolution acquire the stage's basic strength, from hope in infancy to wisdom in old age.

limits: Erikson's stages are a rich and influential framework, but they should be presented with appropriate caution. The ages attached to the stages are approximate and vary between sources and across cultures, so they are best treated as broad periods rather than fixed brackets. The theory is difficult to test empirically, since Erikson drew heavily on clinical and theoretical observation and did not specify precise mechanisms for how crises are caused or resolved, so it is more a descriptive map than a predictive scientific model. It has been criticized as reflecting mid-twentieth-century European and American, and arguably male, assumptions about the ideal life course, limiting its cross-cultural applicability. Erikson himself is often described as a psychoanalyst and developmental psychologist despite having no formal academic degree.
misreadings: Erikson's stages are not rigid age brackets, since the ages are approximate and vary across cultures and individuals. A favorable resolution does not mean eliminating the negative pole, such as all mistrust, but achieving a healthy balance weighted toward the positive. And the theory is not a tightly tested scientific model, being drawn from clinical observation and hard to test, so treating the ages as fixed, resolution as banishing the negative, or the stages as experimentally proven, misreads an influential but approximate lifespan framework.
origin: The eight-stage lifespan theory of the German-American psychoanalyst Erik Erikson, notably in his 1950 book Childhood and Society, extending development across the whole life through a series of psychosocial crises.
